title: ChatGPT produces more “lazy” thinkers: Evidence of cognitive engagement decline
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether using generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, changes students’ cognitive engagement during academic writing. The author frames the problem as a gap in the literature: while large language models are increasingly used in educational contexts, less is known about whether they support or undermine deep thinking, mental effort, attention, and strategic processing during learning tasks. The study focuses on the concern that AI tools may promote cognitive offloading rather than active learning.

To investigate this question, the study used an experimental design with random assignment to two conditions: an AI-assisted group that could use ChatGPT 3.5 during an argumentative writing task, and a control group that completed the same task without AI or other external help. After writing at least 300 words in response to a prompt about integrating AI tools into academic practice, participants completed a newly developed four-item Cognitive Engagement Scale for AI use (CES-AI). The instrument measured self-reported deep processing, effort, sustained attention, and strategic exploration during the task.

The population consisted of 40 adult participants who were current or former students in linguistics, applied linguistics, or related language fields. All were native Greek speakers, had at least a bachelor’s degree, and were affiliated with the University of Nicosia context. The task was completed on an online experimental platform, and participants were monitored through TeamViewer with cameras and screen sharing to ensure compliance with the assigned condition.

The main finding was that the ChatGPT group reported substantially lower cognitive engagement than the control group, with a statistically significant group difference. The author interprets this as evidence that ChatGPT use may reduce mental effort and encourage cognitive offloading in academic writing tasks. The paper concludes that educators should be cautious about uncritical adoption of AI writing support and should design pedagogical strategies that require students to critically evaluate and reflect on AI-generated content rather than passively relying on it.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's large language model chatbot that generates human-like text responses to user prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Participants in the experimental condition used ChatGPT during an argumentative academic writing task for ideas, phrasing, or argument development, then reported their cognitive engagement on the CES-AI.

findings.finding_summary: In a randomized experiment, students using ChatGPT during the writing task reported significantly lower cognitive engagement than the control group. The ChatGPT group scored M = 2.95 (SD = 1.18) on the CES-AI versus M = 4.19 (SD = 0.45) for the non-AI group; the group effect was significant, F(1,38) = 19.2, p < 0.001. The paper interprets this as evidence of reduced mental effort, attention, deep processing, and strategic thinking consistent with cognitive offloading.
findings.measure: CES-AI average score (4-item self-report cognitive engagement scale measuring deep processing, effort, attention, and strategic engagement)

quality_tier_rationale: This is an experimental study with random assignment to ChatGPT versus control, which strengthens causal inference. However, the sample is small (n=40) and the sole outcome is a newly developed self-report scale rather than validated or objective learning measures.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported effect is negative: ChatGPT use was associated with lower cognitive engagement than the control condition. Although the statistical difference is clear, no standardized effect size is reported and the direction is adverse.
